title: Chapter 100 — Leg and Arm
paragraphs: The Pequod, of Nantucket, Meets the Samuel Enderby, of London.
"Ship, ahoy! Have you seen the White Whale?"

Ahab shouted this as he hailed yet another ship, this one flying English colors and bearing down under the stern. The old man stood in his hoisted quarter-boat with the trumpet to his mouth, his ivory leg in plain view of the stranger captain, who was lounging casually in the bow of his own boat. He was a deeply tanned, burly, good-natured, handsome man of about sixty, dressed in a roomy short jacket that hung around him in folds of blue pilot-cloth; one empty sleeve of it streamed out behind him like the embroidered sleeve of a hussar's cloak.
"Have you seen the White Whale?"
"Do you see this?" From the folds that had hidden it, he drew out a white arm made of sperm whale bone, ending in a wooden head like a mallet, and held it up.
"Man my boat!" cried Ahab, impetuously tossing about the oars near him. "Stand by to lower!"

In less than a minute Ahab and his crew, still sitting in their little boat, had been lowered to the water, and they were soon alongside the stranger. But now an odd problem came up. In the excitement of the moment Ahab had forgotten that since losing his leg he had never once boarded any ship at sea except his own, and even then always by means of a clever and very handy mechanical device found only on the Pequod, which could not be rigged up and fitted on another vessel at a moment's notice. Now, it is not at all easy for anyone except people who do it almost every hour, like whalemen, to climb up a ship's side from a boat on the open sea, because the great swells lift the boat high up toward the bulwarks one moment and in the next instant drop it halfway down to the keelson. So, with one leg gone, and the strange ship naturally having none of that thoughtful invention, Ahab found himself miserably reduced to a clumsy landsman again, staring hopelessly at the shifting, uncertain height he could hardly hope to climb.

I may have hinted before that almost every small mishap that came his way as an indirect result of his unlucky injury irritated or infuriated Ahab. This time all of that was made worse by the sight of the strange ship's two officers leaning over the side next to the upright ladder of nailed-on cleats and swinging a pair of prettily decorated man-ropes toward him; at first it did not seem to occur to them that a one-legged man would be too crippled to use their sea-banisters. But this awkward moment lasted only a minute, because the strange captain saw at a glance how things stood and called out, "I see, I see! Stop hauling there! Jump to it, boys, and swing over the cutting-tackle."

As good luck would have it, they had had a whale alongside a day or two before, and the great tackles were still aloft, and the massive curved blubber-hook, now clean and dry, was still attached to the end. This was quickly lowered to Ahab, who at once understanding everything, slid his solitary thigh into the curve of the hook — it was like sitting in the fluke of an anchor, or the crotch of an apple tree — and then giving the word, held himself fast while also helping to hoist his own weight by pulling hand-over-hand upon one of the running parts of the tackle. Soon he was carefully swung inside the high bulwarks and gently landed upon the capstan head. With his ivory arm frankly thrust forth in welcome, the other captain advanced, and Ahab, putting out his ivory leg and crossing the ivory arm — like two swordfish blades — cried out in his walrus way: "Aye, aye, hearty! Let us shake bones together! An arm and a leg! An arm that never can shrink, d'you see, and a leg that never can run. Where did you see the White Whale? How long ago?"

"The White Whale," said the Englishman, pointing his ivory arm toward the east and taking a rueful sight along it as if it had been a telescope, "there I saw him, on the Line (the equator), last season."
"And he took that arm off, did he?" asked Ahab, now sliding down from the capstan and resting on the Englishman's shoulder as he did so.
"Aye, he was the cause of it, at least. And that leg, too?"
"Spin me the yarn," said Ahab. "How was it?"

"It was the first time in my life I had ever cruised on the Line," the Englishman began. "I didn't know anything about the White Whale back then. Well, one day we lowered for a pod of four or five whales, and my boat got fast to one of them. He was a real circus horse, too, going round and round in circles, so that the only way my boat's crew could keep her level was by all sitting with their backsides on the outer gunwale. Then all of a sudden a great bouncing whale comes breaching up from the bottom of the sea, with a milky-white head and hump, all crow's-feet and wrinkles."
"It was he, it was he!" cried Ahab, suddenly letting out his suspended breath.
"And harpoons sticking in near his starboard fin."
"Aye, aye — they were mine — my irons," cried Ahab, exultantly — "but go on!"

"Give me a chance, then," said the Englishman, good-humoredly. "Well, this old great-grandfather, with the white head and hump, runs all foaming into the pod and goes to snapping furiously at my fast-line!"
"Aye, I see! Wanted to part it — free the fast-fish — an old trick — I know him."

"How it was exactly," continued the one-armed commander, "I do not know. But in biting the line, it got foul of his teeth, caught there somehow. But we didn't know it then, so that when we afterward pulled on the line, bounce we came plump onto his hump! — instead of the other whale's, that went off to windward, all fluking. Seeing how matters stood, and what a noble great whale it was — the noblest and biggest I ever saw, sir, in my life — I resolved to capture him, despite the boiling rage he seemed to be in. And thinking the tangled line would get loose, or the tooth it was caught on might pull free — for I have a devil of a boat's crew for a pull on a whale-line — seeing all this, I say, I jumped into my first mate's boat. Mr. Mounttop's here — by the way, Captain: Mounttop; Mounttop: the Captain. As I was saying, I jumped into Mounttop's boat, which was gunwale to gunwale with mine then, and snatching the first harpoon, let this old great-grandfather have it. But Lord, look you, sir — hearts and souls alive, man — the next instant, in a flash, I was blind as a bat — both eyes out — all befogged and bedeadened with black foam, the whale's tail looming straight up out of it, perpendicular in the air like a marble steeple. No use backing off then. But as I was groping at midday with a blinding sun, all crown-jewels — as I was groping, I say, after the second iron to toss it overboard — down comes the tail like a Lima tower, cutting my boat in two, leaving each half in splinters. And, flukes first, the white hump backed through the wreck as though it was all chips. We all struck out. To escape his terrible flailing, I seized hold of my harpoon-pole sticking in him and for a moment clung to that like a sucker-fish. But a breaking wave dashed me off, and at the same instant the fish, taking one good dart forward, went down like a flash. And the barb of that cursed second iron, towing along near me, caught me here" — clapping his hand just below his shoulder — "yes, caught me just here, I say, and bore me down to Hell's flames, I was thinking. When — when — all of a sudden, thank the good God, the barb ripped its way along the flesh — clear along the whole length of my arm — came out near my wrist, and up I floated. And that gentleman there will tell you the rest. By the way, Captain: Dr. Bunger, ship's surgeon; Bunger, my lad: the Captain. Now, Bunger boy, spin your part of the yarn."

The professional gentleman being pointed out so casually had been standing near them the whole time, with nothing in particular to show his gentleman's rank on board. His face was extremely round but serious. He wore a faded blue woolen frock, or shirt, and patched trousers, and until now he had been dividing his attention between a marlinspike in one hand and a pill-box in the other, now and then throwing a critical glance at the ivory limbs of the two crippled captains. But when his superior introduced him to Ahab, he bowed politely and went straight off to do what his captain had asked.
"It was a shockingly bad wound," began the whale-surgeon, "and taking my advice, Captain Boomer here stood our old Sammy —"
"Samuel Enderby is the name of my ship," interrupted the one-armed captain, addressing Ahab. "Go on, boy."

"Stood our old Sammy off to the northward, to get out of the blazing hot weather there on the Line. But it was no use — I did all I could; sat up with him nights; was very severe with him about his diet —"

"Oh, very severe!" chimed in the patient himself. Then suddenly changing his tone: "Drinking hot rum toddies with me every night till he couldn't see to put on the bandages, and sending me to bed, half-drunk, about three o'clock in the morning. Oh, you stars! He sat up with me indeed, and was very severe with my diet. Oh, a great watcher and very dietetically severe is Dr. Bunger. — Bunger, you dog, laugh out! Why don't you? You know you're a precious jolly rascal. — But push ahead, boy. I'd rather be killed by you than kept alive by any other man."

"My captain, you must have by now perceived, respected sir" — said the unflappable, pious-looking Bunger, slightly bowing to Ahab — "is inclined to be humorous at times. He spins us many clever things of that sort. But I may as well say — en passant, as the French remark — that I myself — that is to say, Jack Bunger, late of the reverend clergy — am a strict total abstinence man. I never drink —"
"Water!" cried the captain. "He never drinks it. It gives him a sort of fits. Fresh water throws him into the hydrophobia. But go on — go on with the arm story."

"Yes, I may as well," said the surgeon, coolly. "I was about to observe, sir, before Captain Boomer's humorous interruption, that despite my best and severest efforts, the wound kept getting worse and worse. The truth was, sir, it was as ugly a gaping wound as surgeon ever saw — more than two feet and several inches long. I measured it with the lead line. In short, it turned black. I knew what was threatened, and off it came. But I had no hand in shipping that ivory arm there" — pointing at it with the marlinspike — "that thing is against all rule. That is the captain's work, not mine. He ordered the carpenter to make it. He had that club-hammer there put on the end to knock someone's brains out with, I suppose, as he tried mine once. He flies into diabolical rages sometimes. Do you see this dent, sir?" — removing his hat and brushing aside his hair, exposing a bowl-like cavity in his skull, but which bore not the slightest scar or any token of ever having been a wound — "Well, the captain there will tell you how that came to be. He knows."

"No, I don't," said the captain, "but his mother did; he was born with it. Oh, you solemn rogue, you — you Bunger! Was there ever such another Bunger in the watery world? Bunger, when you die, you ought to die in pickle, you dog. You should be preserved for future ages, you rascal."
"What happened to the White Whale?" Ahab shouted now; up to this point he had been listening impatiently to this byplay between the two Englishmen.

"Oh!" cried the one-armed captain. "Oh, yes! Well, after he sounded, we didn't see him again for some time. In fact, as I hinted before, I didn't then know what whale it was that had served me such a trick, till some time afterward, when coming back to the Line, we heard about Moby Dick — as some call him — and then I knew it was he."
"Did you cross his wake again?"
"Twice."
"But could not fasten?"
"Didn't want to try. Ain't one limb enough? What should I do without this other arm? And I'm thinking Moby Dick doesn't bite so much as he swallows."

"Well, then," Bunger broke in, "give him your left arm as bait to get back the right. Do you know, gentlemen" — bowing very gravely and with mathematical precision to each captain in turn — "do you know, gentlemen, that Divine Providence has built the whale's digestive organs so mysteriously that he cannot possibly digest even a man's arm completely? And he knows it, too. So what you take for the White Whale's malice is only his clumsiness. He never intends to swallow a single limb; he only means to scare you with feints. But sometimes he is like the old juggler, once a patient of mine in Ceylon, who used to pretend to swallow jackknives, and one day actually let one slip down inside him for real. There it stayed for a year or more, until I gave him an emetic and he threw it up in little tacks, you see. There was no possible way for him to digest that jackknife and fully absorb it into his general bodily system. Yes, Captain Boomer, if you are quick enough about it, and are willing to pawn one arm for the privilege of giving the other a decent burial, why, in that case the arm is yours. Just let the whale have another go at you soon, that's all."

"No, thank you, Bunger," said the English captain. "He's welcome to the arm he has, since I can't help it and didn't know him then. But not to another one. No more White Whales for me. I've lowered for him once, and that has satisfied me. There would be great glory in killing him, I know that, and there is a shipload of precious sperm in him. But hark you, he's best let alone. Don't you think so, Captain?" — glancing at the ivory leg.

"He is. But he will still be hunted, for all that. The accursed thing that is best let alone is not always the thing that least allures. He's all a magnet! How long since you saw him last? Which way heading?"

"Bless my soul, and curse the foul fiend's," cried Bunger, stooping and walking round Ahab, and like a dog strangely sniffing, "this man's blood — bring the thermometer! — it's at the boiling point! His pulse makes these planks beat! Sir!" — taking a lancet from his pocket and drawing near to Ahab's arm.
"Back off!" roared Ahab, dashing him against the bulwarks. "Man the boat! Which way heading?"
"Good God!" cried the English captain, to whom the question was put. "What's the matter? He was heading east, I think. Is your captain crazy?" whispering to Fedallah.

But Fedallah put a finger to his lips and slid over the bulwarks to take the boat's steering oar, while Ahab swung the cutting-tackle over to himself and ordered the ship's sailors to get ready to lower.

A moment later he was standing in the stern of the boat, and the Manila men were jumping to their oars. The English captain called after him, but it was no use. Ahab stood upright, his back to the stranger ship and his face set like flint toward his own, until they came alongside the Pequod.
